## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes field procedures for conducting vegetation transect surveys using three common methods: line-point intercept, line intercept, and quadrat (cover class) sampling. These methods quantify plant species composition, percent cover, and community structure across field sites.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Terrestrial vegetation surveys at all EA Program field sites, including the Bernard Field Station, Pomona College Farm, the Pit, restoration sites, and photovoltaic panel study areas
- **Does not apply to:** Aquatic or submerged vegetation surveys; tree-only forest inventory (DBH-based methods); remote sensing vegetation analysis
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve survey design, ensure training compliance       |
| Field Lead        | Coordinate logistics, assign transect locations         |
| Trained Personnel | Conduct surveys, record data, collect voucher specimens |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent surveying          |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Biological:** Poison oak, stinging nettle, ticks, snakes, bees (all common at local field sites)
- **Physical:** Uneven terrain, heat exposure, sharp stakes and rebar
- **Allergenic:** Pollen exposure during peak growing season
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Long pants (required in areas with poison oak or ticks)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (when handling unknown plants)
- [ ] Tick repellent (DEET or permethrin-treated clothing)

### Required Training

- [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd) for emergency response, including allergic reactions and snakebite protocols.


## 5. Summary of Methods

Three survey methods are covered in this SOP. Select the method that best fits your vegetation type and research objectives.

| Method | Best For | Accuracy | Speed | Observer Bias |
|:-------|:---------|:---------|:------|:--------------|
| **Line-point intercept** | Grasslands, herbaceous communities | High | Moderate | Low |
| **Line intercept** | Shrublands, plants with dense canopies >1 m | High | Slow | Low |
| **Quadrat (cover class)** | Mixed communities, rapid assessment, rare species detection | Moderate | Fast | Moderate |

::: {.callout-tip}
### Choosing a Method
For most EA Program projects in southern California grasslands and shrublands, **line-point intercept** is the default method. Use **quadrats** when rare species detection is important or when rapid assessment is needed. Use **line intercept** for shrub-dominated communities where canopy boundaries are distinct.
:::


## 6. Required Materials

### Field Equipment

| Item                          | Notes                                          |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| 50 m measuring tape           | Fiberglass preferred (doesn't stretch)         |
| Chaining pins or rebar stakes | For anchoring transect endpoints               |
| Pin flags                     | For marking transect start/end and quadrat locations |
| Sampling pin or rod           | Thin metal rod (~3 mm diameter) for point intercept |
| 1 m x 1 m quadrat frame      | PVC or metal; for cover class method           |
| Compass                       | For establishing transect bearings              |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording transect coordinates              |
| Field data sheets             | Printed from Appendix A                        |
| Clipboard and pencils         | Mechanical pencils work well in the field      |
| Plant identification guides   | Regional flora; Jepson Manual for California   |
| Camera                        | For photo documentation at each transect       |
| Collection bags and plant press | For voucher specimens of unknown species      |
| Flagging tape                 | For temporary marking                          |

## 7. Estimated Time

| Task                        | Time                                           |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|
| Site preparation and transect setup | 15--30 minutes per transect              |
| Line-point intercept survey | 30--60 minutes per 50 m transect               |
| Line intercept survey       | 45--90 minutes per 50 m transect               |
| Quadrat survey              | 10--15 minutes per quadrat                     |
| Data entry and QC           | 30 minutes per transect (post-field)           |


## 8. Procedure

### 8.1 Survey Timing

Conduct vegetation surveys during the peak growing season for the target community. In southern California:

- **Grasslands and annual forbs:** March through May
- **Coastal sage scrub:** April through June
- **Riparian:** June through August

Consistency in timing across years is essential for detecting temporal changes.

### 8.2 Transect Layout

1. Determine transect locations using the project sampling design (random, stratified random, or systematic placement within habitat zones)
2. Navigate to the starting point and record GPS coordinates
3. Establish the transect bearing using a compass (typically perpendicular to environmental gradients, e.g., slope, moisture, or distance from structures)
4. Anchor the 0 m end of the measuring tape with a chaining pin
5. Walk out the tape to the desired length (typically 50 m), keeping it taut and as straight as possible
6. Anchor the far end with a second chaining pin
7. Photograph the transect from both ends

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo of a measuring tape stretched across a grassland with chaining pins visible -->
<!-- Save as: images/transect_setup.jpg -->

::: {.callout-note}
### Permanent Transects
For long-term monitoring, mark transect endpoints with permanent markers (capped rebar driven flush with the ground, GPS coordinates recorded to sub-meter accuracy). Take a compass bearing and distance to at least two nearby permanent features for relocation.
:::

### 8.3 Method A: Line-Point Intercept

This method estimates percent cover by recording what a vertical sampling pin contacts at regular intervals along the transect.

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Close-up photo of a sampling pin being lowered through vegetation onto the measuring tape -->
<!-- Save as: images/line_point_intercept.jpg -->

1. Begin at the 0 m end of the transect; always work from the same side of the tape
2. At each sampling point (every 0.5 m or 1 m, depending on project design), lower the sampling pin vertically through the vegetation canopy directly over the tape
3. Record each plant species the pin contacts as it descends from the canopy to the ground (**top hit** is the first species contacted; record all species for multi-layer canopies)
4. If the pin does not contact any vegetation, record the ground surface type: bare soil, litter, rock, moss/lichen, or other
5. Record the height (cm) of the tallest species contacted at each point
6. Advance to the next sampling point and repeat

**Calculations:**

$$
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\text{Number of hits for species } i}{\text{Total number of sampling points}} \times 100
$$

Total cover may exceed 100% when canopy layers overlap.

### 8.4 Method B: Line Intercept

This method measures the length of transect tape intercepted by each plant species. Best suited for shrubs and plants with distinct canopy boundaries.

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo showing a tape measure passing under a shrub canopy, with start and end intercept points marked -->
<!-- Save as: images/line_intercept_shrub.jpg -->

1. Begin at the 0 m end of the transect
2. Walk slowly along the tape, noting where each plant canopy begins and ends (intercepts the tape)
3. Record the species, the start point (cm), and the end point (cm) on the data sheet
4. If a gap occurs within a single plant's canopy that is longer than the canopy width on either side, treat it as two separate intercepts
5. Record gaps between plants as the appropriate ground cover type

**Calculations:**

$$
\text{Percent cover for species } i = \frac{\sum \text{intercept lengths for species } i}{\text{Total transect length}} \times 100
$$

### 8.5 Method C: Quadrat (Cover Class)

This method uses visual estimates of cover within fixed-area plots placed at intervals along the transect.

<!-- IMAGE SUGGESTION: Photo of a 1m x 1m PVC quadrat frame placed on the ground with vegetation visible inside -->
<!-- Save as: images/quadrat_cover_class.jpg -->

1. Place quadrats at predetermined intervals along the transect (e.g., every 5 m or 10 m), or at random distances
2. Ensure enough distance between quadrats for them to be independent sampling units (typically at least 5 m apart)
3. For each quadrat, identify every plant species present
4. Estimate percent cover for each species using the modified Daubenmire cover classes:

| Class | Cover Range | Midpoint |
|:------|:------------|:---------|
| 1     | 0--5%       | 2.5%     |
| 2     | 5--25%      | 15%      |
| 3     | 25--50%     | 37.5%    |
| 4     | 50--75%     | 62.5%    |
| 5     | 75--95%     | 85%      |
| 6     | 95--100%    | 97.5%    |

5. Also record percent cover of bare ground, litter, and rock
6. Note the maximum vegetation height (cm) in each quadrat
7. Photograph each quadrat from directly above


## 9. Voucher Specimens

When a plant cannot be identified in the field:

1. Collect a representative sample including leaves, stems, and flowers or fruit if available
2. Place in a labeled collection bag (site, transect, date, collector)
3. Press specimens the same day
4. Identify in the lab using the Jepson Manual or other regional flora
5. Update the data sheet with the confirmed identification


## 10. Quality Control

- Two observers should independently estimate cover for at least 10% of quadrats to assess observer agreement
- Photograph each transect and quadrat for archival verification
- Review data sheets in the field before leaving the site (check for missing entries, illegible writing, and species code consistency)
- Enter data within 48 hours of collection
- Maintain a species list with standardized codes used across all surveys


## 11. Data Management

### 11.1 Field Data Sheets

Use the data sheets in Appendix A. Record in pencil (ink smears when wet). Use Rite in the Rain paper if available.

### 11.2 Data Entry

Enter data into the project spreadsheet or database within 48 hours. Each row should represent one observation (one point, one intercept, or one quadrat-species combination). Required fields:

- Date, site, transect ID, observer
- Method (LPI, LI, or Quadrat)
- Point/interval/quadrat number
- Species (use standardized 6-letter codes: first 3 letters of genus + first 3 of species, e.g., BRODIA for *Bromus diandrus*)
- Cover value or hit/no-hit
- Height (cm)
- Ground cover type (if applicable)


## 12. Waste and Site Impact

- Remove all flagging tape, pin flags, and temporary markers after the survey
- Do not trample vegetation outside the immediate transect corridor
- Leave permanent markers flush with the ground to avoid hazards to people and wildlife
- Pack out all trash and supplies


## 13. References

- Daubenmire, R.F. (1959). A canopy-coverage method of vegetational analysis. *Northwest Science*, 33, 43--64.
- Elzinga, C.L., Salzer, D.W., & Willoughby, J.W. (1998). *Measuring and Monitoring Plant Populations*. BLM Technical Reference 1730-1.
- Herrick, J.E., Van Zee, J.W., Havstad, K.M., Burkett, L.M., & Whitford, W.G. (2005). *Monitoring Manual for Grassland, Shrubland and Savanna Ecosystems*. USDA-ARS Jornada Experimental Range.
- Baldwin, B.G. et al. (Eds.). (2012). *The Jepson Manual: Vascular Plants of California*. 2nd ed. University of California Press.


## 14. Training Record

Before conducting vegetation surveys independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd) in full
2. Demonstrate familiarity with at least 20 common species at the study site
3. Participate in a supervised survey using each method to be employed
4. Demonstrate acceptable inter-observer agreement on cover estimates (within one cover class for quadrats, or within 5% for line-point intercept)
5. Be signed off by the field lead or PI
